input:
The task is to compute the half-life of a reaction which proceeds according to first-order kinetics, together with the fraction of the reactant which remains after 60 min has elapsed.

For a reaction of the first order, the rate constant k (min-1) determines the half-life t1/2 (min) through the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, whilst the fraction of reactant remaining after a time t (min) is given by exp(-k t). The half-life may be understood as the time taken for the amount present to fall to one half of the amount with which the interval began, and it is a characteristic feature of first-order behaviour that this time is the same at every stage of the decay, the rate being at all times proportional to the amount which remains.

The rate constant has been measured as k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, the value resting upon concentration measurements taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min. Substituting into the relations set out above, we accordingly obtain t1/2 = 10 min, whilst the fraction remaining after 60 min works out at 0.02.

It will be observed that the results hang together in the manner which the definition leads one to expect: following the elapse of one half-life the fraction remaining is one half, and each successive half-life halves the fraction yet again, so that the residue surviving at the stated time is a small one, exactly as the computed figure indicates. It must, however, be emphasised that these relations are peculiar to a reaction of the first order; a reaction obeying a different order follows a different law of decay, and neither the half-life nor the fraction remaining can be carried across to such a case.
target:
Compute the half-life of a first-order reaction, and the fraction of the reactant remaining after 60 min.

For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after a time t (min) is exp(-k t). The half-life is the time in which the amount falls to one half of the amount at the start of the interval. The half-life of a first-order reaction is the same at every point of the decay, because the rate is proportional to the amount present: each interval of one half-life removes the same fraction of what the interval began with, however much that is. The temperature is stated with the rate constant because the constant belongs to the reaction at that temperature and at no other.

The measured rate constant is k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Substitution in the two relations gives t1/2 = 10 min, and the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.02.

The measurement run covers many half-lives, so the decay is followed from the initial concentration down to a small residue, and the rate constant is fitted over the whole course of the reaction rather than over its opening alone. The results are consistent with the definition of the half-life: after one half-life the fraction remaining is one half, and each further half-life halves the fraction again, so the residue at the end of the stated time is small, as the computed fraction states. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life nor the fraction remaining transfers to it.
